```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE,comment="#>",message=FALSE)
library(fastglm)
```

Outcomes such as satisfaction or symptom severity have a natural ordering, but the differences between their categories need not have a numerical interpretation. Treating three severity levels as the numbers one, two, and three imposes equal spacing. An ordinal model instead estimates the probabilities of the ordered categories. We begin with a proportional-odds model, examine how mean bias reduction changes its estimation, and use category probabilities to summarize associations. Alternative cumulative links allow the probability model to reflect different distributional shapes.

# The cumulative-logit model

For categories numbered from lowest to highest, the default model fitted by `fastglm_ordinal()` is

\[
\operatorname{logit}\{\Pr(Y_i\leq j\mid x_i)\}
=\alpha_j-x_i^\mathsf{T}\beta-o_i,
\qquad j=1,\ldots,K-1.
\]

The thresholds \(\alpha_j\) divide the outcome scale, and \(o_i\) is an optional offset whose coefficient is fixed at one. A common slope vector \(\beta\) applies to all thresholds. Consequently, a one-unit increase in a predictor multiplies the odds of an outcome above any threshold by the same factor, \(\exp(\beta_r)\). This common odds ratio gives the model its name. It does not imply equal changes in category probabilities.

Positive slopes shift probability toward higher categories under this sign convention, which also agrees with [`MASS::polr()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/MASS/html/polr.html). The thresholds already specify the model's location, so a separate location intercept would be redundant. Formula fits remove the ordinary model-matrix intercept. A matrix supplied directly must omit that intercept.

# Housing satisfaction

The [housing data in MASS](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/MASS/html/housing.html) describe satisfaction, perceived influence over property management, housing type, and contact with other residents. Each row represents a combination of these variables, and `Freq` gives its number of residents.

```{r}
housing <- MASS::housing
levels(housing$Sat)
c(rows=nrow(housing),residents=sum(housing$Freq))

fit_ml <- fastglm_ordinal(Sat~Infl+Type+Cont,data=housing,
                          weights=Freq,tol=1e-10)
fit_br <- update(fit_ml,firth=TRUE)
summary(fit_br)
```

The response factor supplies the order of the categories. An unordered factor requires an explicit order through `levels`, which avoids interpreting an alphabetical coding as a substantive ordering. The weights here are frequencies: a row with weight ten represents ten observations with the same recorded values. They are retained on that scale rather than rescaled to sum to the number of rows.

Mean bias reduction solves the adjusted score equations developed for cumulative-link models by [Kosmidis (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1111/rssb.12025). These equations target the leading bias of the original thresholds and common slopes. The ordinal adjustment generally does not arise from adding a log-determinant penalty to the likelihood, so the binomial penalized-profile calculations are not applied to this model.

```{r}
cbind(maximum_likelihood=coef(fit_ml,component="location"),
      mean_bias_reduction=coef(fit_br,component="location"))
exp(coef(fit_br,component="location"))
fastglm_diagnostics(fit_br)
```

The exponentiated slopes are common odds ratios. The fitted probabilities below often provide a more direct description of the outcome distribution. The convergence diagnostics report the remaining change proposed by the estimating equations; a returned coefficient vector alone does not establish that those equations were solved. The reciprocal information condition number describes numerical conditioning in the fitting coordinates: values near zero indicate that the information matrix is close to singular. This check concerns the stability of the coefficient calculations, whereas the scores and remaining changes assess whether the fitting equations have been solved.

Housing type has several coefficients. A joint Wald test assesses whether those coefficients are all zero in the specified proportional-odds model. A separate contrast compares high with medium perceived influence.

```{r}
fastglm_wald_test(fit_br,terms="Type")
fastglm_wald_test(fit_br,contrast=c(InflHigh=1,InflMedium=-1))
```

These tests use the estimated coefficient covariance and a first-order chi-square approximation. The same interface accepts an eligible robust covariance through `vcov.`. For mean bias reduction, finite estimates permit the calculation but do not establish small-sample accuracy. Testing whether regression coefficients are zero addresses their contribution to the fitted model; the common-slope tests later in this vignette address whether their effects differ across thresholds.

## Alternative cumulative links

The cumulative-logit model uses the logistic distribution to translate a threshold and predictor value into a cumulative probability. More generally, the model is
\[
\Pr(Y_i\leq j\mid x_i)=G(\alpha_j-x_i^\mathsf{T}\beta-o_i).
\]
The probit link uses the standard normal distribution for \(G\). The complementary log-log link uses \(G(\eta)=1-\exp\{-\exp(\eta)\}\), whose asymmetric shape allows cumulative probabilities to approach zero and one at different rates. All three links retain ordered thresholds and common slopes. Positive slopes shift probability toward higher outcomes under the same sign convention.

```{r}
fit_probit <- update(fit_br,link="probit")
fit_cloglog <- update(fit_br,link="cloglog")
link_models <- list(logit=fit_br,probit=fit_probit,cloglog=fit_cloglog)
link_averages <- do.call(rbind,lapply(names(link_models),function(link) {
    data.frame(link=link,fastglm_average(link_models[[link]],weights=housing$Freq))
}))
rownames(link_averages) <- NULL
link_averages
```

The fits are compared through their category probabilities because their coefficient scales differ. Exponentiated coefficients have the common-odds-ratio interpretation for the logit link. Reversing the outcome order changes a complementary-log-log model, so the declared ordering should reflect the substantive outcome scale.

Mean bias reduction uses the first and second derivatives of the selected cumulative distribution in the adjusted equations of Kosmidis (2014). It targets bias in that link's threshold and slope parameters. The same link is retained by prepared fits, refitting bootstrap calculations, predictions, marginal effects, and model assessment. `fastglm_po_test()` tests the common-slope restriction on the fitted link scale; for probit and complementary log-log models its printed heading identifies that interpretation. These score and Wald tests retain their first-order inferential scope.

# Probabilities and average contrasts

```{r}
profiles <- unique(housing[,c("Infl","Type","Cont")])[1:4,]
pred <- predict(fit_br,newdata=profiles,se.fit=TRUE)
pred
predict(fit_br,newdata=profiles,type="cumulative")
```

The display pairs each profile and outcome category with its estimated probability and standard error. `as.data.frame(pred)` extracts this table, and `pred$fit` retains the original probability matrix, whose rows sum to one. Cumulative predictions give the probability through each category except the last, whose cumulative probability is necessarily one. Prediction standard errors combine uncertainty in the thresholds and slopes using expected Fisher information, the model-based measure of information about these parameters. They assume independent categorical observations and a correctly specified proportional-odds model. These first-order approximations can be unreliable in small or extreme samples.

Average probabilities describe a covariate distribution rather than a single profile. Because the housing rows represent different numbers of residents, the following calculation uses the frequencies again as averaging weights. Fitting weights determine the estimated model; averaging weights determine the population of predictor values over which predictions are summarized.

```{r}
fastglm_average(fit_br,weights=housing$Freq)

low_contact <- housing
low_contact$Cont <- factor(rep("Low",nrow(housing)),
                           levels=levels(housing$Cont))
contact_difference <- fastglm_average(
    fit_br,newdata=low_contact,weights=housing$Freq,
    contrast=function(x) {
        x[,"ContHigh"] <- 1
        x
    })
contact_difference
```

This contrast compares high with low contact while keeping the observed distribution of influence and housing type fixed. Each estimate is a difference in the probability of the named satisfaction category. The differences sum to zero because both sets of probabilities sum to one. These are model-based descriptive comparisons, with uncertainty conditional on the supplied predictor distribution. The reported intervals use a normal approximation and are not truncated to the range of possible probability differences.

## Continuous predictors and local changes

A continuous predictor also permits a local comparison: the rate at which each category probability changes as the predictor increases. This derivative is often called a marginal effect. Its size can vary across observations even when the model has a common slope, because the probabilities depend on the other predictor values. Averaging these derivatives summarizes the local association over a specified predictor distribution.

The housing predictors above are categorical, so their associations are described by discrete contrasts. For a continuous example, we generate an ordered severity outcome from an exposure and a binary group. The quadratic term allows the association with exposure to vary over its range, and the interaction allows that association to differ between groups.

```{r ordinal-marginal-effects}
set.seed(110303)
severity <- data.frame(exposure=runif(500,0,3),
                       group=factor(rep(c("A","B"),250)))
location <- with(severity,.7*exposure-.15*exposure^2+
                  .35*exposure*(group=="B"))
severity$outcome <- ordered(cut(location+rlogis(nrow(severity)),
    c(-Inf,.3,1.6,Inf),labels=c("low","moderate","high")))
severity_fit <- fastglm_ordinal(
    outcome~exposure+I(exposure^2)+exposure:group,
    data=severity,firth=TRUE)
exposure_effect <- fastglm_marginal_effects(
    severity_fit,"exposure",newdata=severity)
exposure_effect
```

The estimates are changes in probability per unit of exposure, averaged over these observations. Multiplying an estimate by a small exposure change approximates the corresponding average probability difference. A full one-unit change can differ appreciably from this local approximation. The effects sum to zero across categories because increases in some category probabilities are accompanied by decreases in others. A positive common slope shifts probability toward higher outcomes, but an intermediate category can gain or lose probability depending on the predictor values.

For formula fits, `variable="exposure"` refers to the original exposure variable. The calculation differentiates its linear term, squared term, and interaction together, using the fitted prediction basis. Matrix fits differentiate the named design column while holding the other columns fixed. Formula derivatives use small centered changes in the predictor; terms must be smooth within each row, and both perturbed values must lie in the transformation's domain. Expressions that recompute sample summaries, such as `I(exposure-mean(exposure))`, are unsupported. Supplying `newdata` is necessary when the original predictor cannot be recovered from the stored model frame. Offsets are held fixed, including offsets expressed as functions of the selected predictor.

The intervals account for uncertainty in the thresholds and slopes through the delta method. They condition on the supplied predictor distribution and averaging weights; frequency weights must be supplied again when those frequencies define the desired average. The `vcov.` argument accepts an alternative coefficient covariance, including an eligible robust covariance from `fastglm_vcov()`. These intervals use a first-order normal approximation and may be unreliable in small or extreme samples.

# Sampling uncertainty and model assumptions

The expected-information standard errors above use the fitted categorical distribution to describe sampling variation. Each observation also contributes a score, which measures how its log likelihood changes as the parameters change. A sandwich covariance combines the observed sensitivity of the score equations with the variation in these individual contributions, as described by [Zeileis (2006)](https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v016i09). This permits a first-order variance estimate under distributional misspecification, provided observations are independent and the fitted parameter has a regular, identifiable population target. Robust standard errors do not correct an incorrect mean or probability model.

```{r}
V_robust <- fastglm_vcov(fit_br,type="HC0")
cbind(model_based=sqrt(diag(vcov(fit_br))),
      sandwich=sqrt(diag(V_robust)))
fastglm_average(fit_br,weights=housing$Freq,vcov.=V_robust)
```

The frequencies represent individual residents. Consequently, the independent-observation calculation accumulates score variability at the resident level, including when residents with the same recorded values share a row. A row with frequency ten contributes ten individual observations to this calculation. For mean-bias-reduced fits, the sandwich uses ordinary likelihood scores and their observed derivative at the bias-reduced estimate. With a fixed number of parameters and a regular, identifiable limit, the score adjustment becomes small relative to sampling variation as the sample size increases. This first-order convention differs from differentiating the complete adjusted equations and does not supply a finite-sample coverage guarantee. The returned covariance records this convention.

When observations belong to independent clusters, `cluster` supplies the cluster identifier for each fitted row. The calculation then uses the sum of score contributions within each cluster, following the construction described by [Zeileis, Köll, and Graham (2020)](https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v095i01). All observations represented by a frequency row must belong to its stated cluster. A large number of independent clusters is needed for the usual approximation; repeated observations within a few clusters do not substitute for additional clusters. Cluster covariance is available through `fastglm_vcov(fit, type="HC0", cluster=cluster_id)`. The current robust interface requires positive observed frequency in every declared category.

A refitting bootstrap describes variation by constructing new response datasets and fitting the model again. In the following parametric bootstrap, predictors and offsets remain fixed, while satisfaction counts are sampled from the fitted category probabilities. The statistic records the common slopes after each refit.

```{r}
boot_location <- fastglm_bootstrap(
    fit_br,R=199,type="parametric",seed=61103,
    statistic=function(fit) coef(fit,component="location"))
boot_location
```

This calculation assumes the fitted response model. The alternatives `type="pairs"` and `type="cluster"` resample stored rows or whole independent clusters, respectively. Row resampling preserves the counts and weights attached to each sampled row; it therefore describes a different sampling scheme from resampling individual residents represented by frequencies. The analyst must choose the scheme that corresponds to the study design. Formula transformations and factor coding are held fixed during refitting. Because parametric draws also preserve predictor rows and total row frequencies, their refits reuse design preparation within each worker process. Each replicate still has its own starting thresholds, optimization, and convergence assessment.

Each replicate records convergence, the empty categories, and whether its empty-category pattern differs from the original. An endpoint is the lowest or highest category of the ordered scale. Mean bias reduction keeps its threshold finite when an endpoint is empty, so the same set of model parameters remains available. For a parametric bootstrap with mean bias reduction, the package returns uncertainty summaries when the original fit and every refit contain all interior categories and all refits and statistics succeed. An empty interior category ties adjacent thresholds and changes the fitted model, so the package withholds summaries in that case. Endpoint-empty refits remain visible in the diagnostics. This exception applies only to parametric bootstrap with mean bias reduction; maximum likelihood and pairs or cluster resampling retain the stricter category requirement. Percentile intervals also have simulation error, so a substantive analysis needs enough refits to estimate the interval endpoints adequately.

# Simulated responses

Simulation from the fitted distribution can help assess the range of category patterns implied by a model. The housing frequencies give the number of residents at each recorded predictor row. `simulate()` therefore returns a list of count matrices, with a simulated count for each satisfaction category at each row.

```{r}
simulated <- simulate(fit_br,nsim=2,seed=61104)
head(simulated[[1]])
all(rowSums(simulated[[1]])==housing$Freq)
```

These counts already include the fitting frequencies. Refitting a simulated count matrix uses unit weights, because applying the original weights again would count the same residents twice. For an individual response with unit frequency in each row, `simulate()` instead returns a data frame of ordered factors. Both forms preserve the declared category order. Simulation conditions on the fitted parameters and does not itself account for estimation uncertainty.

# Repeated responses with common predictors

Several ordered outcomes can share the same predictors, and simulation studies often fit many responses on a fixed design. A prepared ordinal design retains the predictor matrix and its formula transformations, so these calculations can be reused across responses. Each model still estimates its own thresholds and common slopes and has its own convergence assessment.

The following preparation uses the housing predictors for both the observed satisfaction response and the two simulated count matrices above. The observed response uses the resident frequencies as weights. The simulated matrices already contain those frequencies and therefore use unit weights.

```{r}
prepared <- fastglm_ordinal_prepare(
    ~Infl+Type+Cont,data=housing,
    levels=levels(housing$Sat),firth=TRUE)
prepared_original <- fastglm_ordinal(
    prepared,housing$Sat,weights=housing$Freq,tol=1e-10)
all.equal(coef(prepared_original),coef(fit_br),tolerance=1e-8)

repeated <- fastglm_ordinal_batch(
    prepared,simulated,weights=rep(1,nrow(housing)),tol=1e-10)
vapply(repeated,function(fit) fit$converged,logical(1))
predict(repeated[[1]],newdata=profiles)
```

The saved preparation includes centering, scaling, and rank checks. These depend on the predictors and each row's effective frequency, which is its individual frequency weight or the sum of its category counts times its weight. In this example, the effective row frequencies are the same for the observed and simulated responses. Changes to the predictor matrix, effective row frequencies, or standardization control rebuild the saved calculations. Offsets and the allocation of a fixed row total among categories can change while this preparation remains applicable. Category mappings, starting values, and parameter-dependent information are calculated separately for each fit.

Prepared designs can also be saved and restored as R objects. This permits reuse across sessions without retaining a connection to a native fitting process. The following serialization reproduces the first refit using the restored preparation.

```{r}
restored <- unserialize(serialize(prepared,NULL))
restored_fit <- fastglm_ordinal(
    restored,simulated[[1]],weights=rep(1,nrow(housing)),tol=1e-10)
all.equal(coef(restored_fit),coef(repeated[[1]]),tolerance=1e-10)
```

`saveRDS()` and `readRDS()` provide the corresponding file-based operation. Formula expressions that refer to external functions or objects still require those dependencies when constructing a new prediction design. Batch fitting currently processes a list of responses sequentially and retains the full fitted models. An individual response can be refitted with `fastglm_ordinal(prepared, response, ...)`; changing the formula requires preparing the revised design again. Preparation retains a dense design and, when standardization is used, its standardized values; its memory requirement therefore continues to grow with the number of rows and predictors.

# Residual diagnostics

A residual for ordered outcomes should preserve the direction of discrepancy without imposing numerical distances between categories. The probability-scale residual of [Li and Shepherd (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/asr073) compares the fitted probability below the observed category with the fitted probability above it. Its value is positive when the observed category is high relative to the fitted distribution, and negative when it is low.

```{r}
probability_residual <- residuals(fit_br)
head(cbind(probability_scale=probability_residual,
           residuals(fit_br,type="cumulative")))
by(seq_len(nrow(housing)),housing$Infl,function(i)
    weighted.mean(probability_residual[i],housing$Freq[i],na.rm=TRUE))
```

The residuals lie between minus one and one. For a count-matrix response, the probability-scale residual is the mean of the individual residuals within that row. Cumulative residuals compare observed and fitted proportions through each threshold, which can help locate discrepancies in different parts of the outcome distribution. Zero-frequency rows have missing residuals. These are descriptive checks: ordinal probability-scale residuals are generally neither normal nor uniform, and cumulative residual columns are dependent.

For reporting and further analysis, optional `broom` methods retain the distinction between common slopes and thresholds. Exponentiation applies to the slopes and their intervals, yielding common odds ratios; threshold estimates and coefficient standard errors remain on the logit scale.

```{r}
if(requireNamespace("broom",quietly=TRUE)) {
    broom::tidy(fit_br,component="location",conf.int=TRUE,exponentiate=TRUE)
    broom::glance(fit_br)
    broom::augment(fit_br,newdata=profiles,se_fit=TRUE)
}
```

The `.fitted` matrix column from `augment()` contains one probability per category, and `.class` gives the category with the largest fitted probability. Training-data augmentation also includes probability-scale residuals. Supplied covariance matrices can be used in `summary()`, `broom::tidy()`, and average probability contrasts, while the prediction standard errors in this example use expected Fisher information.

# Prediction quality and the common-slope assumption

Good numerical convergence establishes that the estimating equations were solved, but the fitted probabilities also need to describe the outcome distribution adequately. Prediction scores summarize discrepancies, while calibration plots indicate where those discrepancies occur. Assessing predictions on observations excluded from fitting helps distinguish predictive performance from agreement with the training sample.

The housing data contain frequency rows rather than individual records. We randomly divide the residents represented by each row between training and evaluation samples, retaining the same predictor coding. The evaluation frequencies are used only after fitting the training model.

```{r}
set.seed(61105)
training_frequency <- rbinom(nrow(housing),housing$Freq,.7)
evaluation_frequency <- housing$Freq-training_frequency
training_fit <- fastglm_ordinal(
    Sat~Infl+Type+Cont,data=housing,weights=training_frequency,
    firth=TRUE,tol=1e-10)
assessment <- fastglm_ordinal_assess(
    training_fit,newdata=housing,y=housing$Sat,
    weights=evaluation_frequency,bins=5)
assessment$scores
```

The logarithmic loss penalizes assigning small probabilities to observed categories. The ranked probability score sums the squared discrepancies between predicted cumulative probabilities and the individual indicators of an outcome at or below each threshold. Both are proper prediction scores: their expected values are minimized by the true outcome probabilities; see [Gneiting and Raftery (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1198/016214506000001437). Smaller values indicate better predictions for the same outcome scale and evaluation observations. The normalized ranked probability score divides by the number of thresholds, placing its possible values between zero and one. For grouped counts, the calculation averages individual scores; squaring the difference from a grouped observed proportion would measure a different quantity.

```{r, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.5}
plot(assessment,type="calibration")
```

For each threshold, the calibration plot compares the mean predicted probability with the observed proportion at or below that threshold. The bins are equal-width intervals of predicted probability, chosen without reference to the observed outcomes. Points near the diagonal indicate agreement within those bins. Sparse bins can vary considerably, and the frequency column in `assessment$calibration` records the number of observations represented. Empty bins have unavailable observed proportions. These plots are descriptive and can conceal discrepancies within a bin; they do not establish that the full conditional probability model is correct.

The proportional-odds model also assumes that a predictor has the same slope at each threshold. A descriptive comparison fits a separate binary model for an outcome above each threshold, retaining the original predictors and offsets. As illustrated in [Harrell's ordinal regression chapter](https://hbiostat.org/rmsc/ordinal), differences between estimates at different cutoffs can arise from sampling variation even when proportional odds holds. The auxiliary models use mean bias reduction to permit finite estimates in many sparse or separated samples.

```{r, fig.width=8, fig.height=8}
assumption_check <- fastglm_ordinal_assess(fit_br,proportional.odds=TRUE)
head(assumption_check$proportional.odds[
    ,c("category","term","estimate","common.estimate","converged")])
plot(assumption_check,type="proportional.odds")
```

Positive auxiliary slopes describe shifts toward higher outcomes, matching the ordinal model's sign convention. Dashed horizontal lines mark the common slopes from the ordinal fit, and the vertical intervals are separate 95% normal intervals for the auxiliary slopes. Variation across thresholds can suggest that the common-slope restriction deserves further investigation. The estimates use overlapping observations and are correlated, so their displayed uncertainty cannot be interpreted as independent tests of equal slopes. The comparison is a graphical diagnostic, with failed threshold fits retained in the returned table; it does not provide a formal proportional-odds test.

## An analytic test of proportional odds

We can assess the common-slope restriction with `fastglm_po_test()`. The score measures how the log likelihood would initially change if the slopes were allowed to differ across thresholds. Its expected variation is calculated from the category probabilities under the fitted proportional-odds model, with adjustment for the estimated thresholds and common slopes. This calculation uses expected Fisher information, obtained by averaging over possible outcomes analytically. It requires neither simulated outcomes nor resampling to compute a p-value.

```{r}
po_test <- fastglm_po_test(fit_br)
po_test
```

By default, the test refits the proportional-odds null by maximum likelihood, including when the original model used mean bias reduction. The original fitted model and its predictions remain unchanged. The printed table identifies the null estimation method and uses a first-order chi-square approximation. Expected and observed information can give different score statistics in finite samples. The [SAS/STAT description of the proportional-odds score test](https://support.sas.com/documentation/onlinedoc/stat/123/logistic.pdf), on pages 4246 to 4248, allows either form; the implementation here uses expected information throughout.

The same test can be included with prediction scores by calling `fastglm_ordinal_assess(fit_br,po.test="score")`. Printing that assessment displays its scores and test in separate tables. Printing its `proportional.odds.test` component displays the test alone. For a report or subsequent calculation, `as.data.frame(po_test)` and `broom::tidy(po_test)` provide numeric columns with the full computed precision; display rounding does not change those values.

For \(s\) predictor columns and \(K\) categories, the joint test has \(s(K-2)\) degrees of freedom. A small p-value gives evidence against the common-slope model in the specified direction of departure. A large p-value does not establish proportional odds, particularly when the sample contains little information about a category or predictor. The graphical comparison remains useful for understanding which threshold-specific associations differ and whether those differences are substantively important.

We can also select formula terms. The following test allows the slopes associated with housing type to differ across thresholds while retaining common slopes for perceived influence and contact. Selecting a factor includes all of its model-matrix columns.

```{r}
type_test <- fastglm_po_test(fit_br,terms="Type")
type_test
as.data.frame(type_test)
```

The joint p-value is `r signif(po_test$p.value,3)`, and the housing-type p-value is `r signif(type_test$p.value,3)`. Neither comparison gives strong evidence against its specified common-slope restriction in these data. This finding should be considered alongside the plotted associations and the prediction assessment, since limited power can also produce a large p-value.

This selected-term test still assumes that the other terms satisfy proportional odds. It does not fit a model with unrestricted threshold-specific effects for those terms. For a matrix fit, `terms` selects named predictor columns. Within `fastglm_ordinal_assess()`, the corresponding argument is `po.terms`. Frequency weights, grouped category counts, and location offsets follow the same conventions as fitting, without expanding grouped observations.

When several terms are of interest, `by.term=TRUE` provides both the joint test and a separate test for each selected term. The calculations share the null fit and its information, which avoids repeated fitting and passes through the predictor data.

```{r}
po_terms <- fastglm_po_test(fit_br,by.term=TRUE)
po_terms
as.data.frame(po_terms)
```

Each term-specific alternative relaxes only that term's common-slope restriction. The reported p-values are unadjusted for multiple testing; the joint test provides a single assessment of all selected restrictions. Individual results remain accessible through `po_terms$tests`, including explanations for unavailable comparisons.

The chi-square approximation requires independent observations and a correctly specified, identifiable null model with positive category probabilities. It can be inaccurate in small or sparse samples. If a declared category is empty, the design is deficient, the ML null does not converge, or the expected information cannot be used reliably, `available` is false and the statistic and p-value are missing; `reason` and `detail` explain the failure. A finite bias-reduced fit therefore does not guarantee that this ML-based test is available. The function does not silently remove categories or switch tests.

When assessment outcomes are supplied through `newdata` and `y`, the test refits its null to those outcomes using the complete rows with positive frequency. It then assesses proportional odds in that evaluation population. This differs from the prediction scores above, which assess predictions from the original fitted coefficients. Neither calculation establishes independence or correct specification of omitted predictors.

## Separation and a bias-reduced null

When a predictor group contains only the highest outcome, increasing its slope can keep improving the likelihood without reaching a finite maximum. This is a form of separation. Additional iterations cannot produce a finite ML estimate in such a sample. The test checks for this configuration in predictors with two observed values and reports it directly.

```{r}
exposure <- matrix(c(0,1),ncol=1,dimnames=list(NULL,"exposed"))
sparse_counts <- rbind(c(12,18,20),c(0,0,4))
colnames(sparse_counts) <- c("low","middle","high")
sparse_fit <- fastglm_ordinal(exposure,sparse_counts,firth=TRUE)
fastglm_po_test(sparse_fit)
```

An explicitly requested mean-bias-reduced null can provide finite estimates under separation. The test then evaluates the ordinary score at that null and removes the contribution associated with estimating its thresholds and common slopes. This removal is essential because the ordinary nuisance score is nonzero at a bias-reduced estimate.

```{r}
fastglm_po_test(sparse_fit,null.estimation="meanBR")
```

This option has the same first-order chi-square limit under a regular interior null, but it can be conservative in small samples. It is an ordinary efficient-score calculation at a bias-reduced null, rather than the larger-model adjusted-score statistic discussed by [Kosmidis (2014, Section 12)](https://doi.org/10.1111/rssb.12025). A higher-order accuracy claim would require a separate justification. The choice of null estimator should be specified as part of the analysis; the function never switches estimators automatically. Within `fastglm_ordinal_assess()`, use `po.estimation="meanBR"` together with `po.test="score"`.

Bias reduction does not supply information about a predictor level that is entirely absent. Empty declared outcome categories and deficient designs therefore remain explicit unsupported cases for these tests. Failed null fits retain their convergence details. The printed explanation can be exported with `as.data.frame(result,details=TRUE)`.

# Empty categories and the declared outcome scale

An outcome category can be absent from a sample even when it belongs to the intended scale. Removing an empty endpoint before bias reduction changes that scale. The following example retains an unobserved low category.

```{r}
no_predictors <- matrix(numeric(),nrow=1,ncol=0)
endpoint_counts <- matrix(c(0,8,2),nrow=1,
                           dimnames=list(NULL,c("low","middle","high")))
endpoint_fit <- fastglm_ordinal(no_predictors,endpoint_counts,firth=TRUE)
coef(endpoint_fit,component="threshold")
predict(endpoint_fit)
```

Bias reduction retains finite thresholds in this example. Maximum likelihood would require an infinite threshold for the empty endpoint, which the current implementation does not estimate.

The same endpoint can be empty in a parametric bootstrap refit. This does not remove a threshold from the mean-bias-reduced model. The bootstrap can report uncertainty when the interior category remains represented in every refit:

```{r}
endpoint_boot <- fastglm_bootstrap(
    endpoint_fit,R=199,type="parametric",seed=61105)
endpoint_boot
data.frame(
  `Category pattern`=c("Empty endpoint","Empty interior category"),
  `Proportion of refits`=c(mean(lengths(
    endpoint_boot$diagnostics$empty.end.categories)>0),
    mean(endpoint_boot$diagnostics$boundary)),check.names=FALSE)
```

For this seed, the low category is empty in some refits, but the middle category is present in every refit. The threshold parameters keep the same meaning throughout this bootstrap. If the middle category were absent, its two neighboring thresholds would coincide and the package would withhold the full-model intervals.

An empty interior category has a different consequence. We fit the reduced category model and restore the declared labels with coincident thresholds and zero probability for the removed category. This boundary interpretation follows the empty-category discussion in Kosmidis (2014, Section 8.3).

```{r}
interior_counts <- matrix(c(4,0,7,3),nrow=1,
                           dimnames=list(NULL,c("low","mild","moderate","high")))
interior_fit <- fastglm_ordinal(no_predictors,interior_counts,firth=TRUE)
coef(interior_fit,component="threshold")
predict(interior_fit,se.fit=TRUE)
diag(vcov(interior_fit))
```

The warning identifies the reduction, and the fitted object records the mapping. The tied thresholds have unavailable Wald standard errors, as does the probability of the removed category. A zero fitted gap does not justify ordinary uncertainty calculations for that gap. Other probability and cumulative-probability standard errors refer to the reduced category model. The convergence checks also use its parameters, because separate score components for the tied thresholds need not vanish at this boundary.

# Computation and scope

The numerical kernel evaluates likelihoods, scores, and information in C++. It processes probability calculations in blocks and avoids constructing a separate regression-design row for each observation and threshold. The dense input design is still retained in memory. Increasing the number of predictors or categories also increases the size of the parameter information matrix.

The current interface supports cumulative logit, probit, and complementary log-log links, freely estimated thresholds, common slopes, offsets, and frequency data. An ordered factor records individual outcomes; a count matrix records the category frequencies within each predictor row. Its columns must follow the declared category order. Sparse and repeatable-source fitting and nonparallel slopes require additional implementations.

`logLik()` reports the ordinary categorical frequency likelihood at the returned estimate, omitting constants introduced by grouping observations. In contrast, `deviance()` compares the fit with a saturated model for the supplied response rows, so the grouped deviance depends on that grouping. For bias-reduced estimates, the reported likelihood is evaluated at those estimates rather than maximized by them.

Model-based inference uses expected Fisher information and normal approximations. Robust covariance and refitting bootstrap calculations have the regularity and category-support requirements described above. Ordinal profile intervals are not supplied. Nonconverged fits retain their diagnostics and point predictions, while methods requiring a covariance refuse to report uncertainty. These distinctions are useful when deciding whether a fitted distribution is sufficiently well determined for the intended interpretation.
